entities.name: Jama Masjid, Delhi
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Jama Masjid of Delhi is India's largest mosque, built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan between 1644 and 1656 CE at the same time as the Red Fort, creating the heart of his new capital Shahjahanabad (old Delhi). Capable of holding 25,000 worshippers, the mosque with its three marble domes, two 40-meter minarets of red sandstone and marble, and broad courtyard is the supreme achievement of Mughal mosque architecture.

Shah Jahan, builder of the Taj Mahal, commissioned the Jama Masjid as the principal Friday mosque of his imperial capital, spending 1 million rupees (an enormous sum) and employing 5,000 workers over 12 years. The mosque stands on a natural rocky hill, elevated above the city on a broad plinth, requiring 36 broad stairs to ascend. Three immense gates open on north, south, and east; the main eastern gate was reserved for the Mughal emperor's exclusive entry.

The mosque houses several sacred relics: a Quran written by the son of Tamerlane, a sandal of the Prophet Muhammad, and strands of his beard. The sandstone and white marble construction creates the red-white contrast characteristic of Shah Jahan's architecture, echoed in the Taj Mahal and Red Fort. Today the mosque conducts Friday prayers attended by over 25,000 people, Eid prayers filling the entire courtyard with 100,000+ worshippers, and serves as the religious heart of Delhi's Muslim community.
